structure.title: Preface and Attunement · Four retellings before the argument
structure.text: Johannes imagines several fathers making Abraham's journey to sacrifice Isaac. Each scene preserves outward features of the biblical story while changing what father or son experiences. Their differences expose how little the bare outline tells us about faith.

structure.title: Eulogy on Abraham and Preliminary Expectoration · Praise and a preliminary difficulty
structure.text: The speaker can admire Abraham and can describe giving up what one loves most. What he struggles to conceive is faith's further movement, the expectation of receiving the beloved in this very life after relinquishing every claim.

structure.title: Problema I–III and epilogue · Duty, the individual and silence
structure.text: The same journey is tried under three questions. Could an ethical duty ever be suspended? Could an individual stand in an absolute relation to God? What could Abraham possibly say to the people whose trust his departure puts at risk?

people.name: Abraham
people.role: The father commanded to sacrifice his son
people.text: God tells him to take Isaac to Mount Moriah, and he rises early and goes, telling no one why. The book keeps retelling that three-day journey, asking whether anyone who admires Abraham has understood what he did.

people.name: Johannes de silentio
people.role: The pseudonymous admirer who cannot follow
people.text: He insists on the distance between understanding resignation and understanding Abraham. His declared limits matter whenever his admiration becomes so eloquent that it sounds like possession of the faith he describes.

people.name: The tragic hero
people.role: A public comparison for a solitary father
people.text: A hero who gives up a child for the city's sake can at least explain the terrible exchange to fellow citizens. Abraham's predicament grows more frightening where that kind of intelligible justification disappears.

prerequisites.title: Genesis, chapter 22
prerequisites.text: The whole book meditates on the story of God telling Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. It is only nineteen verses long; Kierkegaard retells it several ways and assumes you know the original.

context.title: The story in Genesis 22
context.text: God commands Abraham to offer Isaac, the son through whom the promise of descendants is to continue. Johannes dwells on the journey before its outcome. Knowing the familiar ending can make the time the father spends travelling almost disappear.

notice.text: Notice what one altered gesture does to a retelling.
notice.why: A glance, a posture or a father's expression can change the son's whole inheritance. Johannes makes a minute change in the scene bear a theological difference the bare sequence of events cannot show.

notice.text: Listen for examples drawn from ordinary happiness.
notice.why: A knight of faith may be intensely interested in the dinner waiting at home. Johannes tests whether faith can be recognised by outward signs, especially when its object is a thoroughly earthly pleasure.

opening: Abraham takes his son up a mountain intending to obey God's command to sacrifice him. The story is familiar enough to be told reverently without much alarm. Kierkegaard restores the alarm. From outside Abraham's faith, his intention looks monstrous; from inside it, he is supposed to be exemplary. The book keeps returning to the journey and the silence between father and son, refusing to let religious admiration become an easy way of avoiding what the person being admired was prepared to do.
